case_info.scenario: A 17-year-old male with an unremarkable medical history presented with 2 days of painless blurred vision in the right eye. Three weeks prior, he was admitted with fever, myalgias, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and truncal rash. Laboratory evaluation revealed leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Heterophile antibody test results were negative. He recovered with supportive treatment. On examination, the patient was well appearing. His best-corrected visual acuity in the affected right eye was 20/25 and baseline count fingers in the left, secondary to amblyopia. His intraocular pressures were normal and extraocular movements were full. Examination was notable for 1+ anterior chamber cell in the right eye. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye revealed vitreous cell and a supratemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) abutting the fovea. Multiple retinal nerve fiber layer infarcts were observed bilaterally throughout the posterior pole and retinal periphery. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated multifocal areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion, more so in the right eye than the left. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye showed loss of inner retinal laminations, presumably due to intracellular swelling of the ganglion cell layer within areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion (Figure 1). Late vascular staining appeared limited to venules at the boundary of perfused and nonperfused retina and scattered areas of capillary nonperfusion. The patient denied intravenous drug use or antecedent trauma.

case_info.caption: A, Optical coherence tomography (OCT) through the white retinal lesions (pink line) shows focal inner retinal thickening (pink arrowheads). The blue line denotes the OCT through the macula, highlighting loss of inner retinal organization temporal to the macula due to ischemia from the retinal circulation. B, The corresponding fluorescein angiography with white arrowheads highlights the peripheral retina nonperfusion associated with the branch retinal artery occlusion. The insert shows a late-stage frame at 12 minutes with vascular staining and leakage.
case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. 1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration

   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).

case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).

case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.

     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

4. Frustration

case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).

[Case]
A 17-year-old male with an unremarkable medical history presented with 2 days of painless blurred vision in the right eye. Three weeks prior, he was admitted with fever, myalgias, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and truncal rash. Laboratory evaluation revealed leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Heterophile antibody test results were negative. He recovered with supportive treatment. On examination, the patient was well appearing. His best-corrected visual acuity in the affected right eye was 20/25 and baseline count fingers in the left, secondary to amblyopia. His intraocular pressures were normal and extraocular movements were full. Examination was notable for 1+ anterior chamber cell in the right eye. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye revealed vitreous cell and a supratemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) abutting the fovea. Multiple retinal nerve fiber layer infarcts were observed bilaterally throughout the posterior pole and retinal periphery. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated multifocal areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion, more so in the right eye than the left. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye showed loss of inner retinal laminations, presumably due to intracellular swelling of the ganglion cell layer within areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion (Figure 1). Late vascular staining appeared limited to venules at the boundary of perfused and nonperfused retina and scattered areas of capillary nonperfusion. The patient denied intravenous drug use or antecedent trauma.

case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).
